title: The Well at the World's End — Walthamstow to Kelmscott
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: The Boy in Armour — Walthamstow and the Forest

stops.name: Elm House, Walthamstow — the birth
stops.campa: On the twenty-fourth of March a boy is born at Elm House in Walthamstow, above the Lea valley on the skirt of Epping Forest, first surviving son of a City bill-broker grown suddenly rich. The house stands comfortable and Evangelical, hung with the certainties of the age of iron. Into this counting-house world the child comes with the wrong century in his blood, already turned backward toward a time not yet named. On the twenty-fifth of July they carry him to St Mary's to be christened. The nurse remarks that so small a thing should carry so loud a temper.
suggested_refs: William Morris Gallery (Water House), Walthamstow
St Mary's Church, Walthamstow — baptism site

stops.name: Woodford Hall and Epping Forest — the toy suit of armour
stops.campa: The family removes to Woodford Hall, fifty acres against the ancient forest, and here the boy's true kingdom opens. He is given a pony and a small suit of armour made to his size, and in it he rides out under the hornbeams of Epping as a knight of the Table Round, doing battle with tales out of Malory and the Arabian Nights. He reads Gerard's Herball and learns the names of flowers as another child learns catechism. The green shade, the churches of Essex, the brasses on their floors — the whole matter of his life is already laid down in this forest, waiting.
stops.quote: I was born at Walthamstow in Essex in March 1834, a suburban village on the edge of Epping Forest, and once a pleasant place enough, but now terribly cocknified and choked up by the jerry-builder.
stops.quote_source: Morris, autobiographical letter to Andreas Scheu, 5 September 1883
suggested_refs: Morris's childhood pony-armour anecdote (Mackail, Life of Morris)
Epping Forest, Woodford

stops.name: Marlborough College — the boy called Crab
stops.campa: At thirteen he is sent to the new school at Marlborough in the Wiltshire chalk, where the boys nickname him Crab for his sidelong temper and his sudden rages. The teaching is poor and he teaches himself: he walks out over the downs to Avebury and Silbury Hill, reads the antiquities in the school library, and stores up churches and standing stones. He comes away, he will say, knowing a good deal of English Gothic architecture and very little else. The chalk country's barrows and grey sarsens sink into him as the forest had.
suggested_refs: Marlborough College, Wiltshire
Avebury stone circle and Silbury Hill

segments.name: The Brotherhood — Oxford and the Revelation

stops.name: Exeter College, Oxford — the meeting with Burne-Jones
stops.campa: In January he comes up to Exeter College meaning to take holy orders, and on the first day meets a poor clergyman's son from Birmingham named Edward Jones. In an instant a friendship is struck that neither death nor forty years will break. They read Ruskin and Tennyson and Malory together, they walk the Oxford churches, and slowly the Church they came to serve gives way to another faith — Art, and the Middle Age. About them gathers a company of Birmingham men who call themselves the Brotherhood and vow, half in earnest, a Crusade and Holy Warfare against the age.
stops.quote: the memory of that first evening of our lives together... we were both settled in our purpose, and gave up the church for art.
stops.quote_source: Georgiana Burne-Jones, Memorials of Edward Burne-Jones
suggested_refs: Exeter College Chapel, Oxford
Burne-Jones and Morris, joint portrait photographs

stops.name: The Nature of Gothic — Ruskin read at Oxford
stops.campa: That summer the third volume of Ruskin's Stones of Venice appears, and in it the chapter On the Nature of Gothic. Morris reads it and it comes upon him, he will say all his life, with the force of a revelation. Here is the whole gospel he has been groping toward: that the workman's freedom is written in the roughness of the carved stone, that the machine and the division of labour make slaves and dead things, that a man's joy in his work is the measure of its worth. He will one day print the chapter at his own press as a scripture of the age.
stops.quote: you must either make a tool of the creature, or a man of him. You cannot make both.
stops.quote_source: John Ruskin, 'The Nature of Gothic', The Stones of Venice (read by Morris, later printed at Kelmscott Press 1892)
suggested_refs: Kelmscott Press edition of Ruskin's 'The Nature of Gothic' (1892)
The Stones of Venice, first edition

stops.name: Street's office and Red Lion Square — architecture abandoned for art
stops.campa: He is articled to the Gothic architect G. E. Street at Oxford and befriends the head clerk, Philip Webb. When the office moves to London he goes too, and in November takes rooms with Burne-Jones at 17 Red Lion Square. But he has met Rossetti now, who declares that a man should paint, not build, and Morris — who worships him — throws over architecture within the year. Unable to buy furniture he can bear to look at, he has 'intensely medieval' chairs and a great settle made to his own design, and the doctrine of his life is born: that a man should make the things he lives among.
stops.quote: Have nothing in your houses that you do not know to be useful, or believe to be beautiful.
stops.quote_source: Morris, 'The Beauty of Life', lecture at Birmingham, 19 February 1880
suggested_refs: 17 Red Lion Square, Holborn
Morris's medieval settle and chairs (early Firm furniture)

stops.name: The Oxford Union murals — La Belle Iseult and Jane Burden
stops.campa: Rossetti gathers a band of enthusiasts to paint the new Union debating-hall with scenes from Malory. Morris takes for his bay How Sir Palomydes loved La Belle Iseult with exceeding great love, and loved not again; he paints it clumsily but roofs it with a heaven of leaves and flowers, for design is already his true gift. That autumn, at the Oxford theatre, Rossetti spies a stablekeeper's daughter of terrible dark beauty — Jane Burden — and sets her to sit for Guenevere. Morris paints her as Iseult and, unable to draw her rightly, writes upon the back of the canvas: I cannot paint you, but I love you.
stops.quote: I cannot paint you, but I love you.
stops.quote_source: Morris, inscription on the back of his canvas of Jane Burden (La Belle Iseult), 1857–58
suggested_refs: Oxford Union murals (1857–59)
'La Belle Iseult' (Queen Guenevere), Tate — Morris's only surviving easel painting

segments.name: The Palace of Art — Red House and the Firm

stops.name: St Michael at the North Gate, Oxford — the marriage to Jane
stops.campa: On the twenty-sixth of April he marries Jane Burden in the little Saxon-towered church of St Michael at the North Gate, a plain ceremony, the poet Dixon officiating. The stableman's daughter becomes mistress of a household of art; her face — long throat, heavy waved hair, brooding eyes — will look out from the tapestries and the painted glass of two generations, the very type of the Pre-Raphaelite queen. Behind the marriage stands already the shadow that will fall: Rossetti's love for her, and hers for him. But this April day the medieval dream seems whole.
suggested_refs: St Michael at the North Gate, Oxford
Rossetti's many drawings and paintings of Jane Morris

stops.name: Red House, Bexleyheath — the medieval dream made a home
stops.campa: Philip Webb builds for the newly-married Morris a house of red brick in an orchard of Kent, all steep gables and pointed arches, a house that hides nothing and is honest as bread. Morris calls it the Palace of Art. He and his friends fall on it like happy craftsmen: Burne-Jones paints the walls, Jane and the women embroider hangings, Webb designs the very fire-dogs and glasses. Here the guests play at bowls and hide-and-seek in the long garden, and apples fall through the studio windows onto the drawing-boards. It is the medieval commonwealth of makers dreamed at Oxford, briefly and joyfully real.
stops.quote: the beautifullest place on earth.
stops.quote_source: Edward Burne-Jones, of Red House (recorded by Georgiana Burne-Jones, Memorials)
suggested_refs: Red House, Bexleyheath (National Trust)
Webb's Red House furniture and painted settle

stops.name: 8 Red Lion Square — the founding of the Firm
stops.campa: On the eleventh of April the prospectus of Morris, Marshall, Faulkner & Co. goes out — Fine Art Workmen in Painting, Carving, Furniture and the Metals — a brotherhood turned business, with Morris, Rossetti, Burne-Jones, Webb, Madox Brown and the rest as partners. They mean nothing less than to reform the whole look of the English house: stained glass for the churches, painted furniture, embroideries, tiles, and the papers for the wall. Next year at the great Exhibition they win medals; the critics jeer at the medievalism and then, one by one, the churches and the drawing-rooms of England begin to fill with their work.
stops.quote: the lesser arts of life... people would not endure to live in a house that was not, or that they did not think was, beautiful.
stops.quote_source: Morris, 'The Lesser Arts', lecture 1877
suggested_refs: Morris, Marshall, Faulkner & Co. prospectus (1861)
'Trellis' and 'Daisy' wallpapers, Morris & Co.

stops.name: The stained glass — light through leaded saints
stops.campa: The first great success of the Firm is in coloured glass. Burne-Jones draws the figures — long-limbed angels, grave saints, kings out of legend — and Morris chooses and leads the colours, mosaicking the light itself so that a plain village church suddenly burns with the deep blues and rubies the Middle Age knew and the age of factories had forgotten. Windows go into churches across England, and into Jesus College and Christ Church at Oxford. The workman's joy Ruskin preached is here made literal: no window the same, every quarry cut and set by a man's living hand.
stops.quote: the true secret of happiness lies in the taking a genuine interest in all the details of daily life.
stops.quote_source: Morris, 'The Aims of Art' / lectures on work and pleasure
suggested_refs: Morris & Co. and Burne-Jones stained glass, Jesus College Oxford
Christ Church Cathedral windows, Oxford

stops.name: The Earthly Paradise — the idle singer at Queen Square
stops.campa: From the rooms over the shop at Queen Square pours a great river of verse. The Earthly Paradise appears — four-and-twenty tales of Greek and Northern myth told by wanderers who sailed west seeking a land where none grow old, and found it not. In its Apology Morris names himself the idle singer of an empty day, a dreamer of dreams born out of his due time; but the age reads him hungrily and would make him Poet Laureate. The medieval palace of Red House is given up in 1865, never revisited; the marriage darkens; and the poetry becomes the room he can live in.
stops.quote: Dreamer of dreams, born out of my due time, / Why should I strive to set the crooked straight?
stops.quote_source: Morris, 'Apology', The Earthly Paradise (1868)
suggested_refs: The Earthly Paradise, first edition (F. S. Ellis, 1868–70)
26 Queen Square, Bloomsbury

segments.name: The Grey Minster of Lands — the Icelandic Pilgrimages

stops.name: Kelmscott Manor — heaven on earth, and the flight north
stops.campa: In the summer of 1871 Morris takes the lease of a grey gabled Elizabethan manor by the young Thames near Lechlade — Kelmscott, which he calls heaven on earth, a house grown up out of the soil and the lives of those who lived on it. He takes it jointly, in a strange bitter arrangement, with Rossetti, who loves Jane; and then, as if fleeing his own house of grief, Morris turns his back on it within weeks and sails for Iceland. The old walls, the barn, the roses and the tapestried rooms will hold him at the last, but first he must go to the world's cold edge.
stops.quote: a heaven on earth; an old stone Elizabethan house... and such a garden! close down on the river, a boat house and all things handy.
stops.quote_source: Morris, letter to Aglaia Coronio, 1871
suggested_refs: Kelmscott Manor, Oxfordshire (Society of Antiquaries)
Kelmscott Manor frontispiece to News from Nowhere (Kelmscott Press, 1893)

stops.name: The Faroes and the first sight of Iceland — out of the world
stops.campa: The Diana beats north through the grey Atlantic and puts in among the Faroe Islands, black cliffs walling green shelves of turf where the little wooden town of Thorshavn clings above the sea. Morris, a plump prosperous Englishman leaving comfort behind, feels the ordinary world drop away; he writes of the strange solemn beauty, the sense of sailing off the edge of the known. Then on the thirteenth the long coast of Iceland lifts out of the water — the ice-mountain Vatnajökull hanging pale above the black shore, the land of the sagas rising, at last, real before his eyes.
stops.quote: the whole thing was rather solemn than beautiful... I felt as if some old chapter of the Sagas were opening before me.
stops.quote_source: Morris, Icelandic Journals (1871)
suggested_refs: Tórshavn, Faroe Islands
First sight of Vatnajökull from the sea

stops.name: Reykjavík — landfall in the saga-land
stops.campa: On the fourteenth of July the mail-steamer Diana brings him into Reykjavík. With him ride his Icelandic co-translator Eiríkr Magnússon, his old Oxford friend Charles Faulkner, and young Evans; before them a train of ponies and the whole map of the Family Sagas he has taught himself to read in the original tongue. He steps ashore into a treeless grey world under enormous light and calls it, in his journal, our pilgrimage. The sagas he has Englished are no longer books to him; he has come to walk their ground and stand where their dead men fell.
stops.quote: the glorious simplicity of the terrible & tragic, but beautiful land with its well remembered stories of brave men... came upon me with a great shock.
stops.quote_source: Morris, Icelandic Journals (1871)
suggested_refs: Morris's Icelandic Journals, black notebooks
The mail-steamer 'Diana'

stops.name: Þingvellir — the floor whose tomb is time past
stops.campa: They ride to Þingvellir, the rift-valley where for a thousand years the Icelanders met in open parliament, the Althing, upon the Law-Rock between the sundered walls of the earth. Here Njáll spoke and Gunnar was outlawed; here the whole nation once turned Christian in a day. Morris stands in the cleft of the black lava with the great lake beyond and feels the weight of dead law and dead speech under his feet. This is the grey minster of lands whose floor is the tomb of time past — the phrase will come to him among these stones.
stops.quote: Ye who have come o'er the sea to behold this grey minster of lands, / Whose floor is the tomb of time past, and whose walls by the toil of dead hands / Show pictures amidst of the ruin of deeds that have overpast death.
stops.quote_source: Morris, 'Gunnar's Howe above the House at Lithend', Poems by the Way (written after 1871)
suggested_refs: Þingvellir National Park, the Almannagjá rift
The Lögberg (Law-Rock)

stops.name: Bergþórshvoll — the burning of Njáll
stops.campa: Across the flat marsh-lands of Rangárvellir he rides to Bergþórshvoll, the low knoll where the wise Njáll and his sons were burned alive in their hall by their enemies, and where Njáll's wife Bergthóra would not come out but lay down with her husband under an ox-hide to die. Morris stands on the grassy mound with the sea-wind over it and the story alive in him as fact: he can all but smell the smoke. Of all the saga-sites this moves him most — the tragic, terrible, beautiful land, and the courage of men and women who chose their deaths without complaint.
stops.quote: I know how to answer thee well: I will not go out, for I am old, and little fit to avenge my sons, and I will not live in shame.
stops.quote_source: Njáls saga, ch. 129 (the burning), which Morris knew in the original
suggested_refs: Bergþórshvoll, site of the burning in Njáls saga
Njáls saga (Story of Burnt Njal)

stops.name: Hlíðarendi — Gunnar's howe above the house at Lithend
stops.campa: He climbs to Hlíðarendi in the green Fljótshlíð, the home of Gunnar the archer, greatest of Njáll's friends. Here, riding into outlawry, Gunnar's horse stumbled and he turned and looked back at the slope of his home and said the fair hillside had never seemed so fair, and would not go — and stayed, and was killed. Above the house stands the howe, his grave-mound, where legend says he was seen singing merrily in the moonlight after death. Morris stands on the fragrant hayfield slope and understands the man who could not leave his own land, being himself such a man.
stops.quote: Fair is the Lithe; so fair that it has never seemed to me so fair; the corn fields are white to harvest, and the home mead is mown; and now I will ride back home, and not fare abroad at all.
stops.quote_source: Gunnar at Hlíðarendi, Njáls saga ch. 75 (Dasent's rendering, close to Morris's)
suggested_refs: Hlíðarendi, Fljótshlíð — Gunnar's homestead
Morris, 'Gunnar's Howe above the House at Lithend'

stops.name: Geysir and the desert of lava — the volcanic desolation
stops.campa: They come to the great Geysir, the spouting hot spring that gives its name to all such the world over, and camp on the sinter among the steam and the sulphur. Beyond lie the interior deserts — vast fields of black lava and grey ash, glaciers hanging over them, rivers to be forded that could drown a man and his pony together. Morris, the lover of green England, is undone and remade by this desolation. The saga-land's harshness teaches him what abundance costs; the socialism to come is seeded here, among a poor people living nobly on a hard earth.
stops.quote: the most romantic of all deserts... I think I was never so much moved by anything so little to be caught hold of.
stops.quote_source: Morris, Icelandic Journals (1871)
suggested_refs: The Great Geysir and Strokkur, Haukadalur
Icelandic lava-field and glacier photographs

stops.name: The second pilgrimage — Grettir's country and Sigurd Englished
stops.campa: In 1873 he returns, riding the northern quarter, the country of Grettir the Strong and of the Laxdæla folk, Bjarg where Grettir was born and the fells where he was hunted for twenty years. Out of these two journeys and his labour with Magnússon comes the great work: Sigurd the Volsung, the tale of the Northern Achilles and the cursed gold and the dragon Fáfnir, Englished into a rolling epic Morris holds the best thing he ever made. The North has given him a sterner music than the Earthly Paradise, and a myth of doom that will outlast his idle-singer days.
stops.quote: This is the Great Story of the North, which should be to all our race what the Tale of Troy was to the Greeks.
stops.quote_source: Morris, preface note to The Story of Sigurd the Volsung (1876)
suggested_refs: The Story of Sigurd the Volsung and the Fall of the Niblungs (1876)
Bjarg, birthplace of Grettir Ásmundarson

segments.name: The Loom and the Vat — Morris & Co. and the Lesser Arts

stops.name: Queen Square — the wallpapers and the willow bough
stops.campa: Through the earlier seventies, from the workrooms at Queen Square, Morris the pattern-maker comes into his full power. He draws the wallpapers that will hang in half the houses of the world — Trellis with its little birds, Daisy, Pimpernel, and later Willow Bough, the acanthus and pomegranate scrolls — always from the living English hedge and garden, never a dead motif copied from a book. He preaches that the lesser arts, the papers and pots and hangings a man lives among, are the true measure of a civilisation's health, and that no work is worth making unless the maker took joy in the making of it.
stops.quote: If you want a golden rule that will fit everything, this is it: Have nothing in your houses that you do not know to be useful, or believe to be beautiful.
stops.quote_source: Morris, 'The Beauty of Life', lecture at Birmingham, 19 February 1880
suggested_refs: 'Willow Bough' and 'Trellis' wallpapers, Morris & Co.
'Pimpernel' and 'Acanthus' printed designs

stops.name: The Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings — Anti-Scrape
stops.campa: Enraged by the 'restorers' who scrape the honest age off old churches and rebuild them into lifeless copies, Morris founds the Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings, which the trade nicknames Anti-Scrape. Old buildings, he argues, are not ours to falsify; they belong to all the generations that made them and to those not yet born; we are only trustees. It is the first true conservation movement, and its manifesto, in his own hot prose, still governs the care of monuments. The medievalist has become the guardian of the actual medieval stone.
stops.quote: These buildings do not belong to us only... they have belonged to our forefathers, and they will belong to our descendants unless we play them false. They are not in any sense our property, to do as we like with.
stops.quote_source: Morris, SPAB Manifesto (1877)
suggested_refs: SPAB Manifesto (1877)
Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings

stops.name: Merton Abbey Works, on the Wandle — the blue vats and the loom
stops.campa: In June Morris moves the works to Merton Abbey on the river Wandle, seven acres of low sheds among willows and poplar-lined water. Here at last he has room for everything: the great indigo vats sunk in the ground, into which the cloth goes green and comes up, in the air, the true blue that eluded all the age; the high-warp tapestry looms; the stained-glass shop above the dye-house. He dyes with his own blue-stained hands, hunting out the old madder and weld and woad recipes the factories had thrown away. Art, he says, is man's expression of his joy in labour — and here he proves it.
stops.quote: Art is man's expression of his joy in labour.
stops.quote_source: Morris, 'Art under Plutocracy' / 'The Art of the People', lectures (early 1880s)
suggested_refs: Merton Abbey Works, River Wandle
'Cray' and 'Wandle' printed textiles; Morris & Co. tapestries

stops.name: The tapestry loom — the Adoration and the Holy Grail
stops.campa: At Merton the high-warp looms carry the crown of the Firm's work: great arras tapestries woven the old slow way, thread by thread from the back, after cartoons by Burne-Jones with foregrounds of flowers and scrolling acanthus by Morris and Dearle. The Adoration of the Magi goes to the Oxford chapel; the Quest of the Holy Grail, the largest of all, unrolls the whole Arthurian dream of his boyhood in wool and silk. The armour of the toy knight in Epping Forest has become a wall of woven knights; the medieval revelation of Oxford is made, at last, a thing the hands can weave.
stops.quote: the noblest of the weaving arts... in which we may reasonably imitate the earlier work of the Middle Ages.
stops.quote_source: Morris, on tapestry ('Textiles', Arts and Crafts Essays)
suggested_refs: 'The Adoration of the Magi' tapestry (Exeter College chapel)
'The Attainment of the Holy Grail' tapestry series, Merton Abbey

segments.name: The Cause — Socialism and the River to Come

stops.name: The Democratic Federation — crossing the river of fire
stops.campa: On the thirteenth of January, Morris — famous, prosperous, fifty years old — signs the membership card of the Democratic Federation and crosses what he calls the river of fire into revolutionary Socialism. He reads Marx, in French, and confesses he suffered agonies of confusion over the economics but grasped the wrong of it in his bones: that under this system the many toil in ugliness so that the few may waste in luxury. He gives his money, his fame and his failing strength to the Cause, and men who bought his wallpapers are scandalised to see him on soapboxes.
stops.quote: Apart from the desire to produce beautiful things, the leading passion of my life has been and is hatred of modern civilization.
stops.quote_source: Morris, letter to Andreas Scheu, 1883
suggested_refs: Morris's Democratic Federation membership
The Manifesto of the Socialist League (1885)

stops.name: The Socialist League and Commonweal — lecturing in the rain
stops.campa: Splitting from Hyndman, Morris helps found the Socialist League and pours himself into its paper, Commonweal, which he edits and largely pays for. He tramps to open-air pitches on cold Sundays — dock-gates, street-corners, the moor at the edge of grim towns — and preaches Useful Work against Useless Toil to knots of working men, hoarse in the rain, heckled, sometimes arrested. He writes A Dream of John Ball, in which the priest of the 1381 rising speaks across five centuries: that men fight and lose the battle, and the thing they fought for comes about in spite of their defeat, under another name.
stops.quote: men fight and lose the battle, and the thing that they fought for comes about in spite of their defeat, and when it comes turns out not to be what they meant, and other men have to fight for what they meant under another name.
stops.quote_source: Morris, A Dream of John Ball (1888)
suggested_refs: Commonweal, journal of the Socialist League
A Dream of John Ball (Kelmscott Press edition, 1892)

stops.name: Trafalgar Square — Bloody Sunday
stops.campa: On the thirteenth of November the unemployed and the Radicals march on Trafalgar Square in defiance of a police ban, and Morris marches with them. The horse and foot police charge; the crowd is clubbed and scattered; a working man named Alfred Linnell is ridden down and dies of his hurts. Morris walks in front of the vast funeral procession and writes the graveside song, A Death Song, sold to aid the dead man's children — not one man slain but many, killed by the great grey city that grinds the poor. The gentle dreamer of tapestries has learned what the State does to those who ask for bread.
stops.quote: Not one, not one, nor thousands must they slay, / But one and all if they would dusk the day.
stops.quote_source: Morris, 'A Death Song' for Alfred Linnell (1887)
suggested_refs: Bloody Sunday, 1887, Trafalgar Square
Morris, 'A Death Song', with Walter Crane's memorial design

stops.name: Kelmscott House, Hammersmith — News from Nowhere begins
stops.campa: From his Thames-side home at Hammersmith — Kelmscott House, named for the far manor at the river's other end — Morris launches in Commonweal, chapter by chapter from the eleventh of January, News from Nowhere. A man falls asleep in this grimed London and wakes into a green England after the Revolution: no money, no prisons, no factories, no masters; work become pleasure, the Houses of Parliament used to store manure, the Thames clean and salmon-full. It is his whole faith made into a country he can walk through, the utopia that answers all the others — not a machine-paradise but a return to joyful hand-work and fellowship.
stops.quote: Fellowship is heaven, and lack of fellowship is hell: fellowship is life, and lack of fellowship is death.
stops.quote_source: Morris, A Dream of John Ball (1888), the creed of his socialism
suggested_refs: Kelmscott House, Upper Mall, Hammersmith (William Morris Society)
News from Nowhere, first English book edition (Reeves & Turner, 1891)

stops.name: Up the Thames to Kelmscott — the journey through the England-to-come
stops.campa: The dreamer rows up the summer Thames out of Nowhere's Hammersmith, past a cleansed and gardened London, through Runnymede and the locks, into the deep country, until the boat comes at last to the old grey many-gabled house among the elms — Kelmscott itself, the goal of the utopia, the heaven on earth set at the head of the river of time. There the vision fails and he is thrust back into his own harsh century; but he is bidden to go on living to make the dream true. Real England and the England-to-come meet at Kelmscott, and the whole atlas of utopias flows toward this one green door.
stops.quote: if others can see it as I have seen it, then it may be called a vision rather than a dream.
stops.quote_source: Morris, closing words of News from Nowhere (1890)
suggested_refs: The upper Thames, Hammersmith to Lechlade
News from Nowhere ending; Kelmscott Manor as the 'old house'

segments.name: The Ideal Book — Kelmscott Press and the End

stops.name: The Kelmscott Press — the Golden type and the ideal book
stops.campa: In January, in a cottage by his Hammersmith house, Morris founds the Kelmscott Press to make the book a total work of art. He cuts his own types — first the Golden, drawn from the clear Roman of Jenson of Venice, then the Gothic Troy and Chaucer — grinds for the right black ink, hunts down handmade paper and vellum, and designs borders and initials thick as a garden. His aim, with his friend Emery Walker, is the ideal book: type, ink, paper, margin and ornament made one beautiful whole. The first book, his own Glittering Plain, comes off the press in the spring.
stops.quote: I began printing books with the hope of producing some which would have a definite claim to beauty... a book quite unornamented can look actually and positively beautiful.
stops.quote_source: Morris, 'A Note by William Morris on his Aims in Founding the Kelmscott Press' (1898)
suggested_refs: The Golden Type; The Story of the Glittering Plain (1891)
Kelmscott Press ornamental borders and initials

stops.name: The Kelmscott Chaucer — a pocket cathedral
stops.campa: On the second of June the masterpiece is finished: the great folio Chaucer, four years in the making, with eighty-seven woodcuts after Burne-Jones's designs, fourteen huge borders and the ranked initials all from Morris's hand — the printed page become at last the illuminated manuscript's equal and heir. Burne-Jones calls it a pocket cathedral. The two old Oxford brothers, who dreamed at twenty of a Crusade against the age, hold the finished book together, both dying men now, and know the vow is kept. Of all the books of the machine age this is the one made wholly by the joy of the maker's hand.
stops.quote: when the book was done, if we live to finish it, it will be like a pocket cathedral — so full of design and I think Morris the greatest master of ornament in the world.

stops.name: Kelmscott House, Hammersmith — the disease of being William Morris
stops.campa: Worn to nothing by twenty years of doing the work of ten men, he fails through the summer. A great physician, asked the disease, answers that it is simply being William Morris, and having done more work than most ten men. On the third of October, in his Thames-side house at Hammersmith, with the river he loved running past the window, he dies, aged sixty-two, murmuring that he wants to get the mumbo-jumbo out of the world. His doctor says plainly he died a victim of his enthusiasm for spreading the principles of Socialism. The dreamer of dreams, born out of his due time, is done.
stops.quote: I consider the case is this: the disease is simply being William Morris, and having done more work than most ten men.
stops.quote_source: Morris's physician, quoted in J. W. Mackail, The Life of William Morris (1899)

stops.name: Kelmscott churchyard — home to the river at the last
stops.campa: On a wild wet October day they bring him home up the Thames valley to Kelmscott, his heaven on earth. Not in a hearse but on a hay-wain, an open farm-cart wreathed in willow-boughs and vine, drawn by a farm-horse, the country funeral of a man who wished to be one of the country-folk who built his house. They lay him in the little churchyard of St George beneath a simple ridge-roofed stone that Philip Webb will design. The river runs on past the many-gabled house; the England-to-come he dreamed sails, in his book, forever up this water toward this door.
stops.quote: the many-gabled old house built by the simple country-folk of the long-past times.
stops.quote_source: Morris, News from Nowhere (1890), describing Kelmscott, the journey's end
